title: Matot: not while they fight alone (Numbers 32:6)
hook: "Shall your brethren go to the war, and shall ye sit here?"

segments.voice: Yesterday, two tribes said sheepfolds first and children second, and Moses turned the sentence around. Your line was children first.

The group project where one person quietly stops showing up. The family where one sibling does all the hospital visits while the others send texts. Everyone has been on one side of that or the other. Step back to the moment before yesterday's plan. The tribes of Reuben and Gad have just asked to stay on the east side of the Jordan, where the grazing is good, and not cross over with everyone else. Moses' first answer is a single, burning question.
screen: `THE ONE WHO STOPS SHOWING UP.` → `STAY ON THIS SIDE OF THE JORDAN.` → `A SINGLE, BURNING QUESTION.`

segments.voice: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, Moses says: "Shall your brethren go to the war, and shall ye sit here?" Then he goes further. He reminds them of the spies, nearly forty years before, whose fearful report took the heart out of the whole people and cost a generation its chance to enter the land. Your fathers did this, he says, in paraphrase, and now you're doing it again. If you turn away, you'll discourage everyone. The tribes don't storm off. They come back with a better offer: we'll settle our families here, but we ourselves will go armed in front of the others, and we won't return to our homes until every tribe has received its inheritance. Moses accepts. And they kept their word. At the start of the book of Joshua, the men of Reuben and Gad, with half the tribe of Manasseh, cross the Jordan and fight with everyone else. Years later, when the land is settled, Joshua sends them home and praises them: you have not left your brothers all these many days. The rabbis turned Moses' question into a principle. Hillel, in Pirkei Avot, says: do not separate yourself from the community. And the Talmud says that when the community is in trouble, a person shouldn't say, I'll go home and eat and drink, and let things be well with me. The tribes could have had the good grazing and sat it out. They chose to stand with the others first.
screen: `SHALL YE SIT HERE?` · `THE SPIES, NEARLY FORTY YEARS BEFORE.` · `THEY KEPT THEIR WORD.` · `DON'T SEPARATE FROM THE COMMUNITY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone fighting something right now: an illness, a job loss, a hard season with a child, a move, grief. Picture what showing up would actually look like, a meal, a ride, an hour on the phone, sitting with them in a waiting room, and let that picture settle.
Matot. The portion where Moses asks two tribes, shall your brothers go to war while you sit here? And they choose to cross over and stand with them.
Your line: don't sit it out. In Hillel's words, don't separate from the community. Day four hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Moses' question to Reuben and Gad is read in the portion of Matot in summer, and Hillel's teaching 'do not separate yourself from the community' from Pirkei Avot is often studied alongside it.

chat.says: The tribes got the land they wanted. Did they still have to fight?
options: Yes; they went armed in front, and didn't go home until every tribe had land.
No; Moses let them stay home, since they'd already won their share east.
Yes, but only their herdsmen went; the fighters stayed with the families.
chat.meaning: They promised to go armed ahead of the others, and in the book of Joshua they kept their word: you have not left your brothers.

Reuben.meaning: a tribe that asked to settle east of the Jordan

Manasseh.meaning: a tribe; half of it settled east with Reuben and Gad

Hillel.meaning: a sage who said: do not separate from the community

Pirkei Avot.meaning: chapters of the fathers, a book of the sages' sayings
